story.title: Where Should the Chai Go?
story.hook: A chai startup is about to bet its savings on the wrong place. The board deck says so, anyway.
narrative: Kulhad & Co. sells clay-cup chai through an app, and after nine months of sign-ups the founders are ready to open their first real flagship kiosk. Co-founder Tanvi Hegde has a lease draft on her desk in Pune. Her partner, Arjun Nair, keeps muttering that half their regulars seem to live somewhere else.

The investor, a retired banker named Mrs. Lobo, has one rule: the kiosk goes wherever the most customers already are. The board deck's bar chart points firmly at Pune, the tallest bar by a clear margin, and she plans to sign the cheque on Monday.

Arjun has slipped you the raw sign-up export behind that chart. Nobody has checked it since the app went live. Before anyone signs a five-year lease, find the thing in this file that could send the kiosk to the wrong place.

meta.title: Kulhad & Co. App Sign-ups, Jan-Sep 2024
meta.description: Every customer who signed up on the chai app in its first nine months, with where they are and what their first month looked like. One thing in this export would lead a decision badly astray. Find it.

columns.city: string, city the customer entered at sign-up
columns.referral_source: categorical, how they heard about the app
columns.first_order_inr: int, value of the first order in rupees (the app has a 90-rupee minimum order)
columns.orders_first_month: int, number of orders in the first 30 days

story.title: The Tuesday Ledger
story.hook: A yarn shop's weekly orders. The accountant says one thing in here can't be real.
narrative: Marigold & Thread is a two-room shop in a converted bakery that sells hand-dyed yarn online. Every Sunday night Priya exports the week's orders and emails them to her accountant, Mr. Okafor.
This week he replied with a single line: "Something in here can't be real." Then he left for a fishing trip with no signal.

Priya has 600 orders, a tax filing due Monday, and no idea what he meant. She has asked you to go through the ledger before then. Start where any bookkeeper would: the totals, the ranges, the extremes.

meta.title: Customer Orders
meta.description: An e-commerce store exported one week of orders. Something in this export looks wrong -- find it.

story.title: The Spreadsheet That Ate Genes
story.hook: A career-making cancer result, one shared spreadsheet, and 1,400 genes. Something got eaten in transit.
narrative: At the Rao Lab in Bengaluru, postdoc Kavya Menon spent eighteen months growing tumour organoids and sequencing them before and after a new drug. The analysis pipeline spat out a clean table of 1,400 genes, and her collaborator in Leeds, Dr. Tom Hartley, opened it, tidied it up and sent it back for the paper's supplement.

The journal's data editor has now put the submission on hold. Her email is short: 'Several entries in your supplementary table do not correspond to anything in the human genome. Please explain before we proceed.' The editor has not said which entries.

Kavya cannot face telling Professor Rao that a year and a half of work is stuck. She has handed you the exact file Tom sent back. Work out what the editor saw, and whether it can be fixed, before the lab meeting on Friday morning.

meta.title: Organoid Drug Response: Differential Expression
meta.description: A differential-expression table from an RNA-seq experiment: one row per gene, treated vs untreated tumour organoids. It went through a collaborator's hands before submission, and something in it no longer holds up. Find it.

columns.base_mean: float, mean normalised read count across samples
columns.log2_fold_change: float, log2 of treated / untreated expression
columns.lfc_se: float, standard error of the log2 fold change

story.title: The Mangoes Were Perfectly Fine
story.hook: Every truck of Alphonsos arrived at a perfect temperature. So why is Bengaluru sending half of them back?
narrative: Every spring, Deshpande Fruit Co. trucks Alphonso mangoes from the orchards of Ratnagiri and Devgad to wholesalers across India in refrigerated lorries. Sahil Deshpande is the third generation to run it, and this season he paid for new data loggers so no buyer could ever argue about the cold chain again.

Then Mr. Nagaraj, his biggest buyer in Bengaluru, began rejecting crates for bruised, blackened skin. The logger company's glossy report says every single trip was flawless, the insurer will not pay a claim against a flawless record, and Mr. Nagaraj is starting to talk to other growers.

Sahil has sent you the full season's trip log from the new system. He thinks the shiny new dashboard is lying to him but cannot say how, and the season's last trucks leave next week. Find what in this log should never have been believed.

meta.title: Mango Reefer Trip Log, Season 2024
meta.description: One row per refrigerated truck trip from the orchards to a wholesale buyer over the 2024 mango season, as recorded by the new logging system. One thing in this log can't be trusted. Find it.

columns.origin: categorical, packhouse the truck left from
columns.transit_hours: float, hours from loading to unloading
columns.door_openings: int, times the cargo door was opened en route
columns.cargo_temp_c: float, mean cargo-hold temperature over the trip, Celsius
columns.rejected_pct: float, percent of crates rejected by the buyer on arrival

story.title: The Year It Rained Backwards
story.hook: A tea estate's rain gauges say 2023 was a catastrophe. The tea bushes look suspiciously well-watered.
narrative: Kannimala Tea Estate sits above Munnar in the Kerala hills, where three automatic weather stations record every drop the monsoon brings. The estate carries rainfall-index insurance: if the season comes in far below normal, a payout arrives without anyone having to inspect a single bush.

This January the estate's software totted up the year and flagged a disaster, and manager Joseph Kurian filed a claim. Meera Pillai, the insurer's field actuary, drove up to check and found emerald slopes, full check-dams and a very confident manager.

Joseph swears the loggers were never touched. Meera has written the claim off as neither fraud nor fact until someone reads the raw export. She has given it to you. Before anyone is paid, or accused, work out what these numbers are really saying.

meta.title: Kannimala Estate Weather Log 2023
meta.description: Daily observations from three automatic weather stations on a hill tea estate, for every day of 2023. The estate's yearly summary built on this export can't be trusted. Find out why.

columns.station: categorical, one of three estate weather stations
columns.rain_mm: float, rainfall in the 24 hours to 08:30, millimetres
columns.temp_max_c: float, daily maximum air temperature, Celsius
columns.temp_min_c: float, daily minimum air temperature, Celsius

story.title: Too Many People on the Beach
story.hook: A sold-out beach festival let in more people than it sold tickets to. The gate log knows how.
narrative: Saltpan Sound is three nights of music on Morjim beach in North Goa, capped by the police at a strict headcount. Every wristband carries a barcode, and every barcode is scanned once at the gate. Gate lead Rhea Fernandes ran the scanners herself, and they never stopped beeping green.

On the final night a police inspector counted heads, then counted again, and the numbers did not match what the promoter, Kabir Sethi, had sold. Kabir now faces a hearing and a fine that could end the festival for good.

Rhea has exported the entry scan log: one line per wristband that walked through a gate. She believes the answer is sitting in there in plain sight, and the hearing is on Thursday. Find what let the extra people onto the sand.

meta.title: Saltpan Sound 2024 Entry Scans
meta.description: The gate scanner log from a three-night beach festival: one row per wristband admitted, joined to its ticket sale. One thing in this log explains the crowd nobody paid for. Find it.

columns.ticket_id: string, barcode printed on the wristband
columns.purchase_date: date string, YYYY-MM-DD, when the ticket was sold
columns.tier: categorical, Day Pass, Weekend or VIP
columns.price_inr: int, price paid in rupees (early-bird prices are lower)
columns.buyer_state: categorical, Indian state of the buyer
columns.gate: categorical, entry gate where the wristband was scanned
columns.scan_time: datetime string, YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM of the entry scan

story.title: The Register That Read Ahead
story.hook: A lost steamer’s passenger list guesses who came home with spooky precision. Paper isn’t supposed to see the future.
narrative: In April 1913 the steamer Carrow Belle went down in fog off Cape Race with 1,310 souls aboard. A century later the Halifax Harbourfront Maritime Museum is building an exhibit around her, and curator Maeve Lindqvist wants one wall to answer a hard question honestly: what actually decided who lived?

Her volunteer analyst, Jonah Achebe, digitised the shipping company’s register and trained a kiosk model on it. Visitors type in a class, an age, a port, and the screen tells them whether they would have made it home. In testing, it has almost never been wrong.

Maeve is not celebrating. Descendants of the passengers are flying in for opening night on Friday, and she refuses to show them a machine that is right for the wrong reasons. “That register was kept by clerks,” she says, “not by fortune tellers.”

She has handed you Jonah’s table, all 1,310 rows of it, with a pot of museum coffee and a polite warning about the Friday deadline. One thing in it is carrying information that no clerk could have written down on the morning she sailed. Find it before the doors open.

meta.title: Carrow Belle Passenger Register (synthetic)
meta.description: A synthetic reconstruction of a fictional 1913 steamer’s passenger register, one row per passenger, prepared for a survival-prediction exhibit. One thing in this table can’t be trusted as a predictor. Find it.

columns.pclass: int, ticket class (1 = first, 2 = second, 3 = third)
columns.age: float, age in years (blank where the clerk left it empty)
columns.sibsp: int, siblings or spouses travelling with the passenger
columns.parch: int, parents or children travelling with the passenger
columns.fare: float, ticket price in pounds sterling
columns.embarked: text, port of embarkation (S = Southampton, C = Cherbourg, Q = Queenstown)
columns.boat: text, boat code noted in the company register (blank if none)
columns.survived: int, 1 if the passenger survived the sinking, 0 if not (the target)

story.title: Eleven Days From Mars
story.hook: A Mars orbiter keeps arriving lower than planned. Every thruster firing checks out — on paper.
narrative: Cartographer-2 has been coasting toward Mars for ten months. In a windowless operations room in Boulder, Colorado, flight dynamics lead Tamsin Okoro watches the predicted closest approach creep steadily downward, a few kilometres every week, with no single burn to explain it.

Each small thruster firing is written into the log by one of two sources: the spacecraft itself, or a ground model run by a contractor across town. The navigation filter swallows everything. Every row looks perfectly routine on its own, and still the drift keeps growing.

Orbit insertion is in eleven days. If the closest pass sinks much further, the spacecraft will skim the thin upper atmosphere and a $400 million mission becomes a very expensive shooting star. Tamsin’s director wants a real answer, not a hunch, by the morning shift.

You get the full burn log for the cruise, every firing from launch to last Tuesday, and a mug that says WORLD’S OKAYEST NAVIGATOR. Somewhere in this log, the story the numbers tell depends on who is telling it. Find what the navigators are being fed.

meta.title: Cartographer-2 Cruise Burn Log
meta.description: Every thruster firing logged during a fictional orbiter’s ten-month cruise to Mars: angular-momentum dumps (AMD), small trims and trajectory correction manoeuvres (TCM). One thing in this log can’t be trusted. Find it.

columns.date: text, ISO date of the burn
columns.thruster_bank: text, thruster bank used (A or B)
columns.reported_by: text, which pipeline logged the burn (onboard_log or ground_model)
columns.burn_seconds: float, total thruster on-time in seconds
columns.tank_pressure_bar: float, propellant tank pressure at burn time, in bar
columns.impulse_ns: float, total impulse delivered by the burn, in newton-seconds

story.title: The Model That Knew Too Much
story.hook: A salary model scored perfectly on its first try. The CFO doesn't trust perfect.
narrative: Halvorsen Freight hired a consultant to build a model that predicts what each of its 800 employees should earn. On the first run it was flawless. Every prediction landed on the right side of the line.
The consultant sent a celebratory email. CFO Ingrid Halvorsen did not reply to it. She has sat through enough board meetings to know that a perfect model usually means someone let it see the answers.
She has handed you the training table. Somewhere in these columns is a source that knows more than it should. Find it before the model goes live.

meta.title: Employee Salary
meta.description: HR wants to predict 'salary' from the other columns for a compensation model. One of the feature columns is suspicious -- it wouldn't actually be available before you know the answer. Find it.

story.title: Death Cap, Dinner, or Doubt
story.hook: A foraging app is about to tell hikers which mushrooms are dinner. Its five teachers don’t all agree.
narrative: Every autumn the Hollowmere Mycological Society sends volunteers into the damp beechwoods of the Lake District with baskets, knives and clipboards. This year they logged nearly fifteen hundred specimens, each one examined, sniffed, spore-printed and given a verdict at the village hall on Thursday nights.

Society chair Winifred Oakes has struck a deal with a small startup: the survey will train SafeCap, a phone app that looks at a mushroom and tells a walker whether it belongs in the pan. Twenty thousand people have already pre-registered.

The developer, Rafi Castellano, says the model is mostly fine but “strangely confident about exactly the wrong things.” Winifred knows what that means in her hobby. A mistake here is not a one-star review. It is a hospital bed, a liver transplant list, or worse.

She has sent you the full survey export along with a jar of her chanterelle chutney, which she promises is perfectly safe. Five volunteers built this table together over one wet autumn. Something in how it was recorded will poison the app if nobody catches it. Find it before launch.

meta.title: Hollowmere Autumn Fungus Survey
meta.description: Specimens collected by five volunteers over one autumn, with field characteristics and a toxic / edible verdict, exported to train a mushroom-identification app. One thing in this survey can’t be trusted. Find it.

columns.found_on: text, ISO date the specimen was collected
columns.identified_by: text, volunteer who examined the specimen and recorded the verdict
columns.smell: text, dominant smell (none, anise, almond, earthy, foul, fishy)
columns.bruises: text, yes if the flesh bruises when handled
columns.ring: text, yes if the stem has a ring

story.title: The Fridge With Two Witnesses
story.hook: Two thermometers swear 4,000 vaccine doses never warmed up. The inspector has heard perfect alibis before.
narrative: Kowhai Valley Pharmacy is the only chemist for eighty kilometres of Otago sheep country. Every winter it holds the district’s flu vaccines in three medical fridges, and every fridge carries two probes, so that if one thermometer lies, the other can call it out.

Last month a fridge in the next town failed quietly and a whole clinic had to recall its doses. Now inspector Dr Priya Raman is auditing everyone’s logs, and pharmacist Hemi Walker is quietly proud of his: every hour, both probes agreed the vaccines were safe.

Priya is less impressed. Her signature decides whether 4,000 doses go into arms at next week’s school clinics or into a hazardous-waste bin. “Two witnesses are only worth something,” she tells Hemi over a lukewarm cup of tea, “if they didn’t rehearse their story together.”

She has pulled three and a half weeks of the fridge logger’s export, hour by hour for all three cabinets, and handed it to you on a borrowed laptop. One thing in it isn’t what the label on the logger claims it is. Find it before she signs.

meta.title: Vaccine Fridge Logger Export
meta.description: Hourly readings from three vaccine fridges over 24 days. Each fridge has a main probe and a backup probe placed elsewhere in the cabinet, plus room temperature, door-open time and compressor duty. One thing in this export can’t be trusted. Find it.

columns.main_probe_c: float, main cabinet probe temperature in °C
columns.backup_probe_f: float, backup probe temperature in °F (a separate sensor in the cabinet)
columns.door_open_s: int, seconds the door was open during the hour
columns.compressor_duty_pct: float, percent of the hour the compressor ran

story.title: Forty-Five Percent Versus Thirty-One
story.hook: Ashgrove admitted 45% of the men who applied and 31% of the women. The student paper has its scandal. The spreadsheet disagrees.
narrative: Ashgrove University sits on a wet green hill above the river, and for sixty years its graduate school has been quietly proud of itself. Then, on Monday morning, the student paper, The Ashgrove Lantern, ran a front page in red ink: 45% of men who applied for postgraduate places this year were admitted, against just 31% of women. By lunchtime the story was trending nationally.

Provost Dr. Miriam Okafor has a board meeting on Friday and a solicitor's letter on her desk. The Lantern's editor, Callum Reid, a third-year who has never lost an argument, says the numbers speak for themselves. Miriam is not so sure. Every admissions committee she has ever sat on fought about budgets and lab benches, never about whether an applicant was a man or a woman.

She has sent you the full applicant file for the cycle: 2,930 applications, every decision recorded. She has already checked the Lantern's arithmetic, and it is correct. What she needs before Friday is the truth behind it. Find the one thing the headline left out, and name it.

meta.title: Ashgrove Graduate Admissions, 2025-26 Cycle
meta.description: One row per application to Ashgrove's graduate school for the 2025-26 cycle, with the final decision. The pooled figures are being quoted as proof of something. One thing about this file changes what they mean. Find it.

columns.age: int, applicant's age in years at submission
columns.residency: categorical, domestic or international fee status
columns.undergrad_gpa: float, undergraduate GPA on a 4.0 scale
columns.department: categorical, the department the applicant applied to
columns.admitted: int, 1 if offered a place, 0 if rejected

story.title: Nine Crews, One Storyteller
story.hook: Nine film crews. 2,160 cash claims. Forty lakh rupees over budget. Every receipt adds up, and that is what worries the accountant.
narrative: Kaleidoscope Pictures is shooting Suryavansh, the most expensive period epic Mumbai has attempted in a decade. To finish on time, producer Farah Mistry split the film across nine location crews, from the dunes of Jaisalmer to the monasteries of Leh. Each crew runs its own petty cash: chai for two hundred extras, a borrowed elephant, a permit to close a ghat at dawn.

Five months in, the film is forty lakh rupees over budget, and the completion-bond insurer has threatened to take control of the production. Every claim has a receipt. Every category total looks sensible. Farah's finance controller, Ramesh Iyer, has done the books for thirty years, and he keeps muttering the same sentence: "Honest money has a shape."

Ramesh has given you every claim filed this schedule, all 2,160 of them, from nine crews in nine corners of the country. Somewhere in this ledger, money was not spent but written. Find out whose pen it came from before the insurer's auditors land in Mumbai on Monday morning.

meta.title: Suryavansh Petty-Cash Ledger
meta.description: Every petty-cash claim filed by the nine location crews during the first five months of the Suryavansh shoot, one row per claim. The totals look fine and every claim has a reference. Some of these amounts were never really spent. Find out where they come from.

columns.shoot_unit: categorical, the location crew that filed the claim
columns.category: categorical, expense category (catering, transport, lodging, props, costume, equipment_hire, local_permits, misc)
columns.payment_mode: categorical, how the money was paid out (cash, upi, card, bank_transfer)
columns.receipt_attached: categorical, yes/no, whether a scanned receipt is on file
columns.amount_inr: int, claimed amount in Indian rupees

story.title: Hall C Has a Heartbeat
story.hook: Six server racks. Ten days of readings. Every average is textbook, yet disks keep dying in Hall C. Something in there keeps time.
narrative: Merlion Colo occupies four humming floors of a windowless block in Singapore's Jurong East. Hall C is its pride: six racks of servers holding the imaging archive of Tanjong Medical Group, eleven years of X-rays and scans that doctors pull up hundreds of times an hour. For the past month, disks in Hall C have been failing three times faster than anywhere else in the building.

Facility manager Tan Mei Ling has swapped drives, re-seated cables and had the chillers serviced twice. Every dashboard says the hall is fine. Tanjong's CIO has now sent a polite, deadly email: explain the failures by the end of the month, or the four-million-dollar contract moves across the causeway. Mei Ling's night technician, Arjun Pillai, insists the hall sounds different at 3 a.m., as if it were breathing.

Mei Ling has exported ten days of half-hourly telemetry from all six racks. The averages are clean. The histograms are clean. Arjun is sure something isn't. Find what the dashboards are smoothing over, and tell Mei Ling where it lives.

meta.title: Hall C Rack Telemetry
meta.description: Half-hourly telemetry from the six server racks in Merlion Colo's Hall C over ten days in July 2025, one row per rack per reading. Every summary on the dashboard looks healthy. One thing in this log isn't. Find it.

columns.timestamp: string, reading time (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM), every 30 minutes
columns.inlet_temp_c: float, cold-aisle air temperature at the rack inlet, Celsius
columns.outlet_temp_c: float, hot-aisle air temperature at the rack outlet, Celsius
columns.power_kw: float, rack power draw in kilowatts
columns.fan_rpm: int, average server fan speed in the rack
columns.load_pct: float, average CPU load across the rack's servers, percent

story.title: Echoes in the Static
story.hook: An unmanned weather rig in the North Sea. Every chart looks clean. The night engineer says it sounds wrong.
narrative: Station Kestrel is an unmanned weather outpost bolted to a decommissioned rig 90 km off the Scottish coast. A mesh of small devices reports temperature, humidity, pressure and vibration back to shore.
Every dashboard is green. Every histogram is textbook. The data team has signed it off twice.

Only Tomasz, the night-shift engineer, disagrees. He says the station sounds wrong after midnight, "like a record that has started to skip." Nobody believes him. Pull the 1,500 readings and prove him right.

meta.title: IoT Sensor Readings
meta.description: A fleet of IoT devices reports temperature/humidity/pressure/vibration. Nothing looks wrong column-by-column -- but a small group of rows shouldn't be there. Find what's off.
